blocks.markdown: French uses a special "partitive" article for an unspecified quantity of something — roughly "some": **du** (masculine), **de la** (feminine), **de l'** (before a vowel), **des** (plural). *Je mange **du** pain* (I'm eating [some] bread) — Italian and German don't have a direct equivalent; English usually just drops the word entirely.
In a negative sentence, all partitive articles collapse to **de** (or **d'** before a vowel): *Je ne mange pas **de** pain* (I don't eat [any] bread).

exercises.prompt: Je bois ___ eau. (I'm drinking [some] water — eau is feminine, starts with a vowel.)
Il mange ___ fromage. (du — He's eating [some] cheese — fromage is masculine.)
Translate: "I don't eat meat." (negative — partitive collapses to de)
answer: Je ne mange pas de viande.
